units.title: Known versus learned models, system identification and data collection
outcomes: Distinguish a known transition and reward model from a learned one, and state which data each claim rests on.
Fit a one-step dynamics and reward model by supervised regression on fixed interaction data, and report held-out one-step error with the collecting policy named.
Explain why a model fitted under one policy degrades under another, using data coverage.
units.why: Every later planning step trusts a model. This unit fixes what the model is, how it is fitted, and which data earns that trust.

next.note: Roll the fitted model forward and replan.
Plan first against a known model, before blaming learning.

study.title: Chapter 8, Section 8.1: Models and Planning
study.locator: Section 8.1, printed pp. 159 to 160: distribution versus sample models, and what planning may assume
study.depth: Read for vocabulary only. The authors post the full text free at https://incompleteideas.net; the URL above is the publisher page.

focus: A known model is given by the environment (rules, kinematics). A learned model is a supervised fit on transitions collected by some policy, and its promises end where that data ends.
The reward model is learned too. MBPO fits \(p_{\theta}(s'|s,a)\) and \(r\) together by maximum likelihood on the environment dataset.
System identification is regression, not control. Fit first, report held-out one-step error, and only then plan.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, fit \(s' = w_1 s + w_2 a\) by least squares on 200 transitions from \(s' = 0.9 s + a\) plus small Gaussian noise, collected near \(s = 0\) with NumPy seed 2. Recover \(w_1 = 0.9123\) and \(w_2 = 1.0003\) with training MSE 0.00239, then report the MSE on held-out data from the same policy before any planning claim.
traps: Calling simulator access a learned model. A planner that queries privileged state has no sampling error, so its success says nothing about learning.
Reporting training error only. A dynamics fit can memorize its training transitions and still drift off distribution; held-out error under the collecting policy is the minimum report.
Assuming the reward function is known. If the reward is fitted, its error enters every plan exactly like dynamics error.

selfTest.q: What distinguishes a known model from a learned one in one sentence?
selfTest.a: A known model is given independently of data, while a learned model is a supervised fit on transitions collected by some policy and is only trustworthy near that data.

selfTest.q: Why must the collecting policy be named alongside a one-step error?
selfTest.a: The error is measured under that policy's state distribution. A new policy visits new states where the same model can be far worse.

selfTest.q: A model predicts well on average but the planner fails. Name two suspects before blaming the optimizer.
selfTest.a: The planner visits states outside the training distribution, or the failures concentrate in decision-relevant regions that average error hides.

selfTest.q: Does MBPO assume a known reward function?
selfTest.a: No. It learns the reward together with the dynamics by maximum likelihood on the environment dataset.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: known-dynamics sanity case and one-step prediction tests.
units.stopWhen: You can fit a one-step model on fixed data, quote its held-out error with the collecting policy named, and say which states would break it.

fit.note: Berkeley Part 1 and 2, CS224R data slides and Sutton 8.1 cover known versus learned models and data collection at explain and implement depth.

units.title: One-step and multi-step prediction, open-loop rollout and Model Predictive Control
outcomes: Derive a finite-horizon planning objective with a terminal value, and state how its return depends on model and reward error.
Implement open-loop rollout and closed-loop replanning on a small system, and show where they disagree under noise.
Run Model Predictive Control (execute the first action, replan) and explain why the horizon is not the task horizon.
units.why: A model is used by rolling it forward. This unit turns prediction into decisions, and shows why replanning beats blind execution.

next.note: Optimize the finite-horizon objective with shooting and CEM.
Measure how fast the rollout stops resembling the system.

study.title: PETS, Algorithm 1 (MPC loop)
study.locator: arXiv:1805.12114v2, Section 6, Algorithm 1: sample action sequences with CEM, propagate particles, execute only the first action
study.depth: Read the control loop only, not the ensemble training in Sections 4 and 5.

focus: Open loop commits to a whole action sequence from \(s_t\). Closed loop replans after each observation, so feedback corrects prediction error while it is still small.
Planning V2 adds a terminal value \(\hat{V}(\hat{s}_{t+H+1})\) to the \(H\)-step reward sum. Without it a short horizon is myopic; with a bad one it inherits value error.
MPC executes only the first planned action. The planning horizon \(H\) is a compute knob, not the task horizon.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the \(H\)-step objective \(\sum_{t'=t}^{t+H} r(\hat{s}_{t'}, a_{t'}) + \hat{V}(\hat{s}_{t+H+1})\) from the current state, then implement receding-horizon control on a deterministic 1D toy and hand-check one 3-step rollout value before executing the first action.
traps: Executing the full planned sequence in a stochastic system. The later actions were optimized for predicted states, not for the states that occur.
Setting the planning horizon from the task horizon. A short horizon with a terminal value solves long tasks; a task-length horizon with model error solves none.
Dropping the terminal value and calling short-horizon control optimal. It is optimal for the truncated problem, which need not match the task.

selfTest.q: What is the operational difference between open-loop and closed-loop use of the same model?
selfTest.a: Open loop executes the planned sequence without new observations. Closed loop executes the first action, observes the next state, and replans, so feedback corrects drift.

selfTest.q: Why does Planning V2 add a terminal value after the horizon?
selfTest.a: The finite sum alone ignores everything after step \(H\), which makes short-horizon plans myopic. The terminal value estimates the missing tail.

selfTest.q: A planner with \(H = 5\) controls a 500-step task well. Does that contradict the task horizon?
selfTest.a: No. The horizon bounds each lookahead, not the episode. Replanning every step chains short lookaheads across the full task.

selfTest.q: In PETS Algorithm 1, how many planned actions are executed per control step?
selfTest.a: One: the first action of the best CEM sequence. The rest are discarded and planning restarts at the next state.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: prediction tests and planning tests with a known-dynamics sanity case.
units.stopWhen: You can derive the finite-horizon objective with its terminal value, and your receding-horizon loop matches a hand rollout on a deterministic toy.

units.title: Random shooting and cross-entropy planning against a known-dynamics oracle
outcomes: Implement random shooting against a known-dynamics oracle and report its best return with the sample budget stated.
Implement the cross-entropy method (sample, elite refit, repeat) and show it beating shooting on equal samples.
Defend the oracle-plus-simple-controller as the baseline every learned-model result must beat.
units.why: Planning bugs and modeling errors look identical downstream. An oracle planner isolates the first, so later failures belong to the model.

next.note: Replace the oracle with a learned model and account the samples honestly.
Keep the oracle as the planner baseline in the final comparison.

study.title: PETS, CEM versus random shooting
study.locator: arXiv:1805.12114v2, Sections 5 to 6 with the appendix comparison: CEM with 5 iterations of 2500 samples against random shooting on half-cheetah dynamics (Figure A.11), and the horizon note (Figure A.8)

study.title: Lecture 11: Model-Based RL, planning example slide
study.locator: Slide 28: Nagabandi et al. 2019 (ensemble of 3 nets, short-horizon shaped reward, iterative CEM, 30-trajectory alternation)

focus: Random shooting samples \(N\) sequences and keeps the best. CEM fits the next Gaussian to the elite fraction and repeats, so later samples concentrate where returns were high.
The comparison is only fair on equal model queries. CEM with 5 iterations of 2500 samples beats shooting with 2500 samples because it reallocates them, not because it uses more.
The oracle uses true dynamics. Its return is the planner ceiling: a learned model that scores below a simple controller on the oracle has a planning problem, not a modeling problem.
units.reproduce: From a blank file with NumPy seed 0, plan \(s' = s + a\) with reward \(-(s')^2 - 0.01 a^2\) from \(s_0 = 2\) over \(H = 3\) with actions in \([-1, 1]\). Random shooting with 200 sequences scores best value -1.4964 at \([-0.810, -0.990, -0.354]\); CEM with 200 samples and a 20 percent elite reaches elite-mean values -2.4868, -1.2234 and -1.0640 across 3 iterations. Run on CPU and match all four numbers.
traps: Refitting CEM to all samples instead of the elites. The mean then barely moves and the method degrades to shooting with extra steps.
Letting the elite fraction collapse the variance to zero in one iteration. Keep a small variance floor so later iterations can still search.
Presenting the oracle return as a model-based result. It used no learning; it is the baseline, not the achievement.

selfTest.q: Why does CEM beat random shooting on the same total sample budget?
selfTest.a: It spends later samples near the best sequences found so far by refitting the sampling distribution to the elites, while shooting spreads every sample over the initial broad distribution.

selfTest.q: What does PETS Figure A.11 establish, exactly?
selfTest.a: On half-cheetah dynamics, CEM with 5 iterations of 2500 samples plans significantly better than random shooting with 2500 samples. It is the paper's planning comparison on the paper's setup, not a learner target.

selfTest.q: Your learned-model planner scores below random shooting on the true dynamics. What is broken?
selfTest.a: The planner or its budget, not the model: the oracle test removes modeling error, so the gap must come from planning.

selfTest.q: Should the executed action be the first element of the CEM mean or the full mean sequence?
selfTest.a: Under MPC, only the first action, followed by replanning. Executing the full sequence is open loop and forfeits feedback.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: known-dynamics sanity case with planning tests before any learned model.
units.stopWhen: Your shooting and CEM implementations match the four seed-0 numbers, and you can state the oracle return as the planner ceiling for your later model.

fit.note: Berkeley shooting/CEM slides, the PETS planning comparison and the CS224R CEM example cover oracle planning at implement depth.

units.title: Dyna-style imagined experience and imagined versus real accounting
outcomes: Implement tabular Dyna-Q from its boxed steps, including the planning-sampling rule for states and actions.
Reproduce the Dyna maze rank order (more planning steps reach near-optimal behavior in fewer episodes) as the book reports it.
Account imagined and real updates separately, and state the sample budget both ways.
units.why: Dyna is the oldest recipe for turning a model into data. Its loop and its accounting rules recur in every modern imagined-data method.

next.note: See the modern short-rollout form of the same recipe.
Learn what Dyna assumes away: model uncertainty.

study.depth: Steps (d), (e) and (f) of the box are the implementation contract. The authors post the full text free at https://incompleteideas.net; the URL above is the publisher page.

study.title: Lecture 16: Model-Based RL Part 2, Dyna slides
study.locator: Part 2 (Policy learning with models: the Dyna box slide and the general Dyna-style recipe slide)

study.title: Lecture 11: Model-Based RL, Dyna slide
study.locator: Slides 11 to 12: the 4-step MBPO loop labeled as the algorithm called Dyna

focus: Direct RL, model learning and planning run the same update. Step (d) learns from real experience, step (f) replays the identical Q-learning update on imagined experience.
Planning samples a random previously observed state and a random action previously taken there, then queries the stored model. Unseen pairs are never sampled because the model has no entry for them.

With \(n = 0\) the agent is plain one-step Q-learning. The book reports about 25 episodes to near-optimal behavior for \(n = 0\), 5 for \(n = 5\), and 3 for \(n = 50\): rank order on the book's maze, not a learner target.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, implement steps (a) to (f) of the Tabular Dyna-Q box on a small deterministic chain with \(\gamma = 0.95\). Hand-compute one direct update and one planning update for the same transition, and show your code produces both numbers exactly.
traps: Counting imagined updates as environment samples. Report real steps and imagined updates as two numbers; the sample-efficiency claim divides by the first.
Filling unseen model entries with zeros or defaults. The box samples only previously observed pairs; invented entries silently teach invented dynamics.
Keeping the overwrite model of step (e) in a stochastic or changing world. One stored outcome per pair then teaches noise as fact; Exercise 8.5 asks exactly for this failure.

selfTest.q: What does Dyna-Q with \(n = 0\) reduce to, and why?
selfTest.a: One-step tabular Q-learning. Steps (e) and (f) are omitted, leaving acting plus the direct update in step (d).

selfTest.q: State the planning-sampling rule of step (f) precisely.
selfTest.a: Draw a random previously observed state and a random action previously taken in it, look up the stored reward and next state, and apply the Q-learning update.

selfTest.q: Why did larger \(n\) reach near-optimal behavior in fewer episodes on the Dyna maze?
selfTest.a: Each real step funds \(n\) extra Q-learning updates on simulated experience, so values propagate to the start far earlier. The cost moves to compute, not samples.

selfTest.q: What changes in Dyna-Q+ when the world changes, in one sentence?
selfTest.a: Planning updates add a bonus \(r + \kappa\sqrt{\tau}\) that grows with time since the pair was last tried for real, so the agent retests stale transitions.

units.title: Model ensembles, epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty and pessimistic planning
outcomes: Define epistemic versus aleatoric uncertainty, and say which shrinks with more data.
Derive the Gaussian negative log-likelihood for a probabilistic dynamics model and the ensemble disagreement statistic.
Implement a small ensemble, show members disagreeing away from data, and apply an uncertainty penalty in planning.
units.why: A single deterministic model is confidently wrong off data. Uncertainty tells the planner where the model ends and guessing begins.

next.note: See what the planner does with confident errors.
Collect the data that shrinks the epistemic part.

study.title: PETS, uncertainty model and trajectory sampling
study.locator: arXiv:1805.12114v2, Section 4 (probabilistic ensemble: each member outputs a Gaussian) and Section 5.1 (trajectory sampling TS1: one bootstrap per rollout)

study.title: Lecture 11: Model-Based RL, ensemble slide
study.locator: Slide 17: partial rollouts from real states plus an ensemble whose errors average out

focus: Aleatoric uncertainty is noise in the world and stays with infinite data. Epistemic uncertainty is ignorance of the parameters and shrinks where data covers the region.
Each PETS member outputs a Gaussian mean and diagonal variance for \((s', r)\). Disagreement of means across members estimates the epistemic part; the predicted variances carry the aleatoric part.
Pessimism penalizes or constrains plans by uncertainty. Expected value under a high-variance prediction can look fine while the pessimistic value is very low.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, build 3 fixed one-step predictors that agree near training inputs and diverge outside them. At \(x = 0.0\), \(1.0\) and \(3.0\) the prediction standard deviations are 0.0000, 0.0707 and 0.9721: reproduce all three numbers, then derive the diagonal-Gaussian negative log-likelihood your probabilistic member would minimize.
traps: Training every member on identical data with an identical seed. Without initialization or batch diversity the members agree everywhere and the disagreement statistic is theater.
Reading predictive variance as model uncertainty. An output variance can encode pure environment noise; epistemic doubt needs member disagreement or a posterior.
Planning on the ensemble mean as if it were a real dynamics. The mean of plausible models is itself an artificial environment; PETS samples whole rollouts per member (TS1) instead.

selfTest.q: Which uncertainty shrinks with more data, and which does not?
selfTest.a: Epistemic uncertainty shrinks as data covers the region. Aleatoric uncertainty is inherent environment stochasticity and remains with infinite data.

selfTest.q: Why is output entropy alone not enough for model uncertainty?
selfTest.a: It conflates the two kinds: a model can be certain about a noisy world (high aleatoric, low epistemic) or uncertain about a deterministic one (low aleatoric, high epistemic).

selfTest.q: What is TS1 in one sentence, and why not resample a member every step?
selfTest.a: Each rollout keeps one randomly drawn ensemble member for all its steps. Per-step resampling would average members into an artificial dynamics and suppress multimodality.

selfTest.q: What does a pessimistic penalty change about the chosen plan?
selfTest.a: It downweights plans whose predicted return has high uncertainty, steering away from regions where the model may be exploited even when the mean looks good.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: ensemble-disagreement checks and a model-exploitation failure with an uncertainty penalty.
units.stopWhen: You reproduce the three disagreement numbers, derive the Gaussian loss, and can point at a state where your ensemble disagrees and say what the planner must do there.

fit.note: Berkeley Part 3, PETS Sections 4 to 5.1 and the CS224R ensemble slide cover both uncertainties and pessimistic planning at derive depth.

units.title: Compounding error, decision-relevant error and model exploitation
outcomes: Bound compounding one-step error over a horizon under a Lipschitz assumption, and name the three regimes.
Distinguish average prediction error from decision-relevant error with a slice the average hides.
Induce model exploitation on a small task: a plan that scores well in the model and fails in the system.
units.why: Small one-step errors become large trajectory errors, and optimizers seek exactly the states where the model is wrong. This unit makes both effects measurable.

next.note: Use short rollouts to stay on the reliable part of the curve.
Attribute the failure to model, planner, reward or policy.

study.title: Model-Based RL: error recursion
study.locator: A Key Limitation of Dyna: the recursion \(e_{t+1} \le L e_t + \epsilon\) with the three regimes (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Recompute the numbers yourself: with \(L = 1.01\) and \(\epsilon = 0.01\) the exact bounds are 0.01, 0.051, 0.220 and 1.705 at 1, 5, 20 and 100 steps, so the page's 2.7 at 100 steps (which quotes \(1.01^{100}\)) is a slip.

study.locator: Section 8.3, printed pp. 166 to 168: optimistic errors self-correct, pessimistic ones hide; Examples 8.2 and 8.3 with Figures 8.4 and 8.5
study.depth: Read for the exploitation mechanism. The authors post the full text free at https://incompleteideas.net; the URL above is the publisher page.

study.title: MBPO: compounding error and long rollouts
study.locator: arXiv:1906.08253v3, Sections 4.2 and 6.2 with Figure 3: full rollouts compound error, 200-step rollouts underperform short ones, 500-step rollouts fail

focus: With one-step error at most \(\epsilon\) and Lipschitz constant \(L\), the bound after \(T\) steps is the geometric sum \(\epsilon \sum_{i=0}^{T-1} L^i\): convergent for \(L < 1\), linear for \(L = 1\), exponential for \(L > 1\).
Average error weights states by the training distribution. The planner weights them by predicted return, so it migrates to low-data high-reward fantasies the average never sees.
Optimistic model errors self-correct (the plan visits and refutes them). Pessimistic or hidden errors persist: the shortcut maze agent never discovers the path it believes is blocked.
units.reproduce: From a blank file with \(\epsilon = 0.01\), compute the recursion \(e_{t+1} = L e_t + \epsilon\) from \(e_0 = 0\). Match 0.0995, 0.50 and 11.6391 at \(T = 50\) for \(L = 0.9\), \(1.0\) and \(1.1\), and 0.0100, 0.0510, 0.2202 and 1.7048 at \(T = 1\), \(5\), \(20\) and \(100\) for \(L = 1.01\). Run on CPU and match all seven numbers.
traps: Quoting \(1.01^{100} \approx 2.7\) as the 100-step bound. That is the growth factor, not the accumulated error; the geometric sum is 1.7048 at \(\epsilon = 0.01\).
Treating one-step validation MSE as control quality. A model can halve its MSE while its planner gets worse if the remaining error sits on the optimal path.
Testing exploitation with the planner's own imagined returns. Score every candidate plan in the real system (or oracle); imagined scores are the suspect, not the judge.

selfTest.q: State the three compounding regimes and the \(T = 50\), \(\epsilon = 0.01\) bounds.
Why can average error fall while control gets worse?
selfTest.a: Average error weights by training visitation. The planner shifts visitation toward states with high predicted return and thin data, where error can be large despite a good average.

selfTest.q: Why did the blocking-maze agent recover but the shortcut-maze agent not?
selfTest.a: The blocking error was optimistic: the plan tried the phantom path and observed the wall. The shortcut error was pessimistic: the plan avoided the believed-blocked region, so it never collected the refuting observation.

selfTest.q: What is the minimal demonstration of model exploitation?
selfTest.a: A plan whose imagined return exceeds its real return by a margin that grows with optimization pressure, with the gap reproduced across seeds.
